haiku-low.q1: Only a SHA-256 hash (token_hash) is persisted. Plaintext exists only in server memory during create, the create response, and the browser dialog's memory. Never in DB, logs, analytics, URL or localStorage.
haiku-low.q2: They cannot. The token is shown once and nobody, including support and engineering, can reveal it. The user must revoke the lost token and create a new one.
haiku-low.q3: The create is refused with 409 'You have 10 active tokens. Revoke a token first.' Nothing is stored.
haiku-low.q4: On the first request validated after the revoke commits. The revoke call returns only after its commit, and later requests get 401.
haiku-low.q5: Same 401 status, headers and generic JSON body for all three. The responses do not differ; only server logs record the real reason.
haiku-low.q6: It SHA-256 hashes the token and does an indexed lookup on token_hash in Postgres. The row is usable only if revoked_at is null and expires_at is after now().
haiku-low.q7: A successful API request whose stored last_used_at is null or at least 1 hour old triggers a conditional UPDATE after the response. Its WHERE clause stops concurrent requests from stacking writes.
haiku-low.q8: Nothing: the API request still succeeds. The displayed last-used time is a little staler, and the next request retries the write.
haiku-low.q9: It sets revoked_at to now on the row, which is kept, not deleted. The list query filters on revoked_at IS NULL, so the token disappears from the list.
haiku-low.q10: The update matches 0 rows, so the server returns 404. Other users' tokens, unknown ids and already-revoked ids get the same 404, so ids cannot be probed.
haiku-low.q11: The row is committed: the token is live but its plaintext is unknown, it counts toward the limit of 10, and it shows as Never used. The user revokes it and creates a new token.

sonnet.q1: It stores only the SHA-256 hash of the whole token (api_tokens.token_hash, bytea). Plaintext exists only in server memory during the create request, in the 201 create response (Cache-Control no-store), and in the browser dialog's component state until closed.
sonnet.q2: They can't. Nobody (including support and engineering) can show it again and no endpoint reveals it. They must create a new token.
sonnet.q3: The server rolls back and returns 409 with the message "You have 10 active tokens. Revoke a token first." Nothing is stored.
sonnet.q4: On the very next request validated after the revoke commits: Flow 3 finds 0 rows and returns 401. A request validated before the commit may still finish.
sonnet.q5: All get the same 401 with the same status, headers and JSON body. The responses do not differ. Only server logs record the real reason, without the token or hash.
sonnet.q6: It computes SHA-256 of the presented token and looks up api_tokens by token_hash (unique index). The row is usable only if revoked_at IS NULL and expires_at > now() (database clock).
sonnet.q7: An authenticated API request where last_used_at is null or at least 1 hour old triggers a conditional UPDATE setting last_used_at=now, run after the response is sent. The WHERE clause (last_used_at IS NULL OR last_used_at < now - 1 hour) limits it to about one write per token per hour and stops concurrent requests stacking writes.
sonnet.q8: The API request is unaffected and still succeeds. The failure is logged without the token and ignored. The next request retries, and the displayed time is a little staler.
sonnet.q9: It sets revoked_at=now on the row; the row is kept. The list shows only tokens with revoked_at IS NULL and not expired, so the revoked token disappears from the list. It also stops counting toward the limit of 10.
sonnet.q10: The UPDATE matches 0 rows (it requires user_id = session user and revoked_at IS NULL), and the server returns 404. The response is the same for another user's token, a missing id or an already-revoked token, so ids cannot be probed.
sonnet.q11: The row is committed but nobody has the plaintext, and no endpoint can reveal it. The orphaned token is live but unusable, counts toward the limit of 10, and shows in the list as "Never" used. Retrying create with the same name gets 409. The user revokes the orphan and creates a new token. There is deliberately no replay or idempotency key.
